top.line: Two releases passed every check yet never went live
top.para: Two consecutive releases pushed cleanly, verified against both remotes and printed that they were in sync, yet the site served a page two releases old for forty minutes. A human on a phone noticed the version badge. The checks were not weak; they were checking the wrong boundary.

s0.line: A strong hash check proved arrival, not readability
s0.para: The release script builds the site, runs the validator with a vault key tripwire, pushes the encrypted vault and confirms sync, then pushes the git mirror and confirms HEAD matches origin/dev. That last check compares hashes and is strong, but it only proves the bytes reached GitHub, not that anyone can read them.

s1.line: Publishing has three boundaries and only two were verified
s1.para: Publishing runs from source to git remote to Pages deploy to the reader. The release verified the first two boundaries. Between the git remote and the reader sits a GitHub Actions job with its own failure modes, reporting to a system neither remote knows about, which nothing in the release checked.

s2.line: A rate-limited action download killed the deploy job
s2.para: The deploy job died in Set up job when codeload.github.com returned 429 Too Many Requests on actions/configure-pages@v5, failing after 3 attempts. Validation and tagging passed. The most likely deploy failure is not your code but shared infrastructure you do not run, on a day you were not watching.

s3.line: Releases now ask the live site its version
s3.para: Each release now polls the live site with a cache-buster until the new version appears, for up to eight minutes. If it never does, the release aborts loudly, names the Actions page and notes a 429 is transient and needs a re-run. The cost was accepted after two false success reports in one afternoon.

s4.line: Shipped is a fact about the reader, not repositories
s4.para: Three build rules now share one shape: a page nothing links to is unpublished, a page missing from llms.txt is unpublished, and a page the deploy never served is unpublished. Each was learned by getting it wrong first, which keeps the list short and specific rather than long and aspirational.

s5.line: The check detects failed deploys but repairs nothing
s5.para: A 429 still needs a human or a re-run. Only the home page's version badge is checked, so a partial deploy could pass. Each release gains up to eight minutes, a real tax on small fixes. All three are acceptable against the failure replaced; the releases described are v0.2.31 to v0.2.33.
